title: Master of My Fate
text: William Ernest Henley's poem Invictus describes courage under suffering. Its speaker cannot control every event, but claims responsibility for his response. The poem's confidence can inspire perseverance, though real strength also includes seeking help. Courage is not the same as facing every hardship alone.
context: A discussion of an 1875 public-domain poem rather than its full text.
vocabulary: fate: events believed to be beyond control

title: Keeping Your Head
text: Rudyard Kipling's poem If gives advice about patience, courage, risk, and humility. It praises remaining steady when others panic or praise too freely. Some of its ideals reflect the era in which it was written, so a thoughtful reader can admire its discipline while still questioning its assumptions.
context: Commentary on a public-domain poem first published in 1910.
vocabulary: assumption: an idea accepted without proof

title: A Sun That Runs Its Course
text: Ancient Hebrew poetry often uses parallel lines and vivid natural images. In Psalm 19, the heavens communicate through their order, and the sun crosses the sky like a strong runner. The image joins wonder with discipline: reliable movement can be both beautiful and powerful.
context: Literary commentary on a public-domain biblical poem; families may interpret it differently.

title: To Seek and Not to Yield
text: Tennyson's Ulysses imagines the old voyager longing for one more journey. The poem values curiosity and determined effort, but its hero also leaves duties behind. That tension makes the poem worth discussing. Persistence is admirable, yet wisdom asks what our ambitions cost other people.
context: Commentary on Alfred Tennyson's public-domain poem Ulysses.

title: A Ship Reaches Harbor
text: Walt Whitman's O Captain! My Captain! uses a ship returning from a dangerous voyage as a metaphor for the United States after the Civil War. Celebration is mixed with mourning for President Lincoln. Knowing the historical context reveals why victory and grief occupy the same poem.
context: Literary and historical explanation of an 1865 public-domain poem.
source: Original commentary on Walt Whitman's public-domain poem

title: Passing the Lamp
text: Many poems compare teaching to passing a flame or lamp from one generation to another. The image suggests that knowledge does not shrink when shared. A good student receives an inheritance, tests it carefully, and then carries what is true and useful into circumstances the teacher could not foresee.
context: An original prose reflection inspired by traditional poetic imagery.
vocabulary: inheritance: something received from earlier generations

title: Footprints in A Psalm of Life
text: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's “A Psalm of Life” speaks in the voice of a young person who rejects hopelessness. Its steady rhythm urges readers to act in the present, keep working, and leave encouraging “footprints” for others. The poem uses images of marching and battle, but its real contest is the effort to live with purpose. A modern reader can value that energy while asking how rest, patience, and help from other people also support a meaningful life.
context: Original commentary on a public-domain poem; only its title and a single key word are quoted.
vocabulary: purpose: a reason for doing something
rhythm: a repeated pattern of beats
source: Original summary based on Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, A Psalm of Life, Poetry Foundation (public domain)

title: A Home Under the Sky
text: Robert Louis Stevenson's short poem “Requiem” imagines the words the speaker would want above his grave. He pictures a traveler who has finally come home beneath a wide, starry sky. The plain language makes death calm rather than frightening. Because Stevenson traveled often and lived with serious illness, the image of rest carries special weight, yet the poem can stand without biography. It asks readers to consider how a few chosen images can express a whole life's direction.
context: Original commentary on Stevenson's public-domain poem, with no lines reproduced.
vocabulary: requiem: a work honoring someone who has died
biography: the story of a person's life

title: Miniver Cheevy's Imagined Past
text: Edwin Arlington Robinson's “Miniver Cheevy” presents a man who dreams of knights, ancient cities, and famous families while scorning his own time. The jaunty rhythm sounds amusing, but the portrait grows sadder. Miniver blames history and fate instead of changing his habits. His imagined past contains bright armor and glory, not boredom, hunger, or ordinary labor. The poem warns that admiration for history can become an escape from responsibility. Studying the past is most useful when evidence challenges fantasy and helps us act more wisely in the present.
context: Original commentary on a public-domain poem about romanticizing history.
vocabulary: romanticize: make something seem better or grander than it was
source: Original summary based on Edwin Arlington Robinson, Miniver Cheevy, Poetry Foundation (public domain)

title: Wordsworth's Happy Warrior
text: William Wordsworth's “Character of the Happy Warrior” describes courage as a pattern of moral habits, not a thirst for combat. The ideal figure learns from difficulty, controls anger, accepts responsibility, and keeps a generous spirit. Written after the death of naval commander Lord Nelson, the poem uses the public language of heroism. Yet its strongest qualities can apply far beyond war: honest self-command, thoughtful service, and resilience. Readers may also question any portrait of a perfect hero. Real leaders have flaws, and careful judgment should test admired qualities against actual choices.
context: Original commentary on a public-domain poem and its demanding model of character.
vocabulary: resilience: the ability to recover and continue
source: Original summary based on William Wordsworth, Character of the Happy Warrior, Poetry Foundation

references.citation: William Wordsworth, Character of the Happy Warrior, Poetry Foundation

title: A Song That Entered History
text: Julia Ward Howe wrote “Battle-Hymn of the Republic” during the American Civil War, fitting new words to a tune already sung by Union soldiers. Biblical images give the song a sense of judgment and urgent purpose. That power helped it travel into churches, public ceremonies, and later civil-rights gatherings. A historical reading should hold two facts together: the song supported a Union cause increasingly tied to emancipation, and religious certainty can make political conflict sound absolute. Poetry set to memorable music can unite people, preserve hope, and also simplify complicated events.
context: Original historical commentary on a public-domain Civil War poem and song.
vocabulary: absolute: presented as complete and beyond doubt
source: Original summary based on Julia Ward Howe, Battle-Hymn of the Republic, Poetry Foundation (public domain)

title: Power and Humility in Recessional
text: Rudyard Kipling's “Recessional” was written for Queen Victoria's 1897 jubilee, when the British Empire displayed its global power. Instead of offering simple celebration, the poem repeatedly warns that armies, ships, and political glory will pass. Its biblical language calls for humility and remembrance. The warning is real, but readers should also notice what the poem leaves at the edge: people living under imperial rule had their own histories and judgments. Reading critically means hearing the poem's check on pride while placing it beside voices from colonized societies. Context changes analysis; it need not force only one response. A famous work can contain insight without providing a complete view.
context: Original critical commentary on a public-domain poem in its imperial setting.
vocabulary: colonized: placed under the political control of an outside power
source: Original summary based on Rudyard Kipling, Recessional, Poetry Foundation
